title: The Five-Cycle and the Erdős–Hajnal Property

items.title: A bipartite layer is small unless a large comb already appears
items.strategy: For a fixed layer, define the sets P_i and Q_i from the source construction. Mark good vertices backwards so that at least half of the chosen vertices are good by comparing the disjoint P_i with the union of the Q_i. The good vertices then yield a comb unless its width is already too small, and in that remaining case the same inequality bounds the whole layer.

items.title: A bipartite graph with bounded A-degree has a large comb or a small B-side
items.strategy: Partition the B-side into layers according to the geometric degree thresholds (2/3)^s Delta. The previous lemma bounds every layer unless a comb already appears, and summing those bounds gives a geometric series. Hence either a comb exists at some stage or the whole B-side is small.

items.title: A tau-critical graph with a large low-degree induced subgraph has a rooted stable-tooth comb
items.strategy: Starting from the given induced subgraph X, iteratively choose a maximum-degree vertex v_i, its neighbourhood A_i inside the current remainder, a large stable set C_i inside A_i using tau-criticality, and then the next remainder X_i anticomplete to {v_i} union C_i. Apply the bipartite comb theorem to each pair (C_i,D_i) to bound D_i unless the desired rooted comb already appears. If no rooted comb appears, the partition of X into the vertices v_i, the sets A_i, and the sets D_i contradicts the inequality used to choose tau.

items.title: A sparse graph has a prescribed-size induced subgraph of bounded maximum degree
items.strategy: Average the edge count over all subsets of size 2m-1. Some such subset inherits the same sparse edge bound, so fewer than m of its vertices can have degree at least epsilon(m-1). Deleting those high-degree vertices leaves an m-vertex induced subgraph with the required maximum-degree bound.

items.title: An H-free graph has a linearly large induced subgraph whose graph or complement has bounded maximum degree
items.strategy: Use the published edge-density form of Rödl's theorem to get a linearly large set Z whose induced graph or complement has low edge density. After halving the density parameter, shrink to size ceil(delta|G|) with the previous lemma. The resulting set has size at least delta|G| and its induced graph or complement has maximum degree at most epsilon delta|G|.

items.title: A rooted stable-tooth comb with a cross-edge between two blocks contains an induced five-cycle
items.strategy: Take two teeth a_i and a_j, their matched block vertices b_i and b_j, and the root v. The rooted-comb axioms force exactly the adjacencies of the cycle v-a_i-b_i-b_j-a_j-v and exclude all other edges among these five vertices, so they induce C_5.

items.title: The C5-free graphs satisfy a polynomial kappa bound
items.strategy: Fix epsilon below 1/400 and a corresponding low-degree constant delta from the previous corollary, then choose tau small enough that the rooted-comb theorem applies and the final exponent comparison goes through. A minimal counterexample is tau-critical. The bounded-degree corollary gives a large set X in G or in its complement; since C5 is self-complementary, work in the sparse case. The rooted comb theorem gives a rooted stable-tooth comb in G[X], and the previous lemma shows that its blocks must be pairwise anticomplete. Tau-criticality gives a polynomial lower bound for each block, and summing the resulting stable sets contradicts the assumed upper bound on kappa(G).

items.title: The five-cycle has the Erdős-Hajnal property
items.strategy: The previous theorem gives a positive exponent tau with kappa(G) at least |G|^tau on every C5-free graph. The published equivalence between the kappa and homogeneous-set formulations then yields the Erdős-Hajnal property for C5.

title: The Five-Cycle and the Erdős–Hajnal Property — Examples

items.title: A rooted stable-tooth comb with two teeth
items.strategy: Take vertices v, a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2 with edges va_1, va_2, a_1b_1, and a_2b_2, and no others. Then ((a_1,{b_1}),(a_2,{b_2})) is a two-tooth comb, the teeth are stable, and v is adjacent to both teeth while anticomplete to both blocks.

items.title: A cross-edge in a rooted stable-tooth comb creates an induced five-cycle
items.strategy: Add the edge b_1b_2 to the previous five-vertex rooted comb. Then v, a_1, b_1, b_2, a_2 induce the cycle C_5 in that cyclic order.

items.title: A comb can have an edge between two blocks
items.strategy: Use the same two-tooth data as in the previous example. It is still a comb in the bare sense, but the edge b_1b_2 shows that pairwise anticompleteness of the blocks is not built into the definition.

items.title: FALSE: every comb has pairwise anticomplete blocks
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the previous counterexample. The anticomplete-block conclusion on the A page uses the extra rooted stable-tooth structure together with C5-freeness, not the comb definition alone.
